objective: Where could software create a meaningful baseball advantage for the Chicago Cubs? The current date is early October 2026, in the Cubs' offseason (their 2026 season ended in the Wild Card Series). A prior experiment found that triaging the November minor-league free-agent pool offers little: the low-attention pool holds under one next-season contributor per club per year, and a simple 'played in MLB last year' rule already finds most value. Prefer recurring decisions where the value at stake is large enough to matter, where public information available at decision time could plausibly beat a simple rule, and where a retrospective test on public history is possible. Consider front office, player development, scouting, coaching and business-of-baseball decisions, and name where software is unnecessary or clubs are already ahead. OUTPUT GUIDANCE (format only): Each IDEA names one problem, the decision owner, the concrete recurring decision and its timing, the size of value at stake, the mechanism of advantage, the simple baseline a club already uses, and the software intervention. Follow with ASSUMPTION and UNKNOWN lines. Do not invent statistics or private Cubs information.
text: IDEA: Qualifying offer decisions; owner: GM/president of baseball operations; decision: whether to extend a qualifying offer to each eligible departing free agent, made yearly in the days after the World Series; value at stake: a one-year salary at the QO amount if accepted versus a compensation draft pick if declined; mechanism: estimate acceptance probability and market AAV from public signals at decision time (age, recent WAR, injury history, agent, market depth at the position) instead of a binary rule; baseline: offer when expected market AAV clearly exceeds the QO amount; software: a calibrated acceptance and market-value model backtested on public QO outcomes since the system began.

assumptions: The QO decision may overlap previously explored arbitration or free-agent commitment families, so its novelty needs checking before investment.
Public QO history has few cases per year, so a model may not separate from an experienced executive's judgment.
The value of the compensation pick depends on the club's revenue-sharing and tax status under the CBA, which must be verified rather than assumed.
The decision only recurs when the club qualifies, so annual expected value is discounted by playoff probability.
Counterfactual roster value cannot be observed directly, so the retrospective test relies on simulation that may embed the same biases it is meant to test.
Contending clubs likely already run such simulations internally, which would make the edge small.
Coach effects may be confounded by roster turnover, front-office philosophy, and regression to the mean, making them unidentifiable from public data.
Public staff records may be incomplete or inconsistently dated, especially for assistant and minor-league roles.
This is unconventional precisely because it may not work, and a null result would itself be useful for avoiding overpaying for perceived coaching reputations.
The per-attempt run value is small, so a season-level gain may be a fraction of a win.
Leading clubs likely already exploit this, which would leave limited edge.
Pitcher time-to-plate data may not be fully public, which would weaken the model.
This may overlap the explored travel and rest planning family, which would need deduplication.
The effects of rest days are confounded by selection, since teams rest pitchers who already show fatigue.
The value is probably small and clubs likely already have such tools, so this may be a case where software adds little.
Catcher framing value is likely to shrink under the ABS challenge system, so framing-based catcher decisions should be checked against the explored ABS family.

Coaching hire evaluation; owner: president of baseball operations and manager; decision: hiring or retaining major-league and upper-minors hitting, pitching, and assistant coaches, made mainly in October and November; value at stake: staff who may influence many players at once across multiple seasons; mechanism: estimate a coach-associated change in player outcomes (for example plate discipline or pitch-mix shifts) from public data across all clubs when coaches move between organizations; baseline: reputation, referrals, and interviews; software: a coach-movement panel built from public staff announcements linked to player-level Statcast changes, with controls for aging and regression.

Stolen-base attempt policy under pitch-clock and disengagement limits; owner: manager and first-base and third-base coaches; decision: green-light or hold calls by runner, pitcher, catcher, count, and disengagement state, made every game; value at stake: run expectancy from many attempts over a season; mechanism: combine public sprint speed, catcher pop time, pitcher pickoff and disengagement history, and count to estimate break-even success probability in each situation; baseline: give fast runners a standing green light and hold everyone else; software: a situational attempt chart, backtested on public play-by-play and Statcast baserunning data since the 2023 rule changes.

Rotation sequencing around off-days; owner: manager and pitching coach; decision: whether to keep a strict rotation order, skip a starter, or insert a sixth starter around scheduled off-days, made weekly during the season; value at stake: allocation of starts among starters of different quality, plus fatigue costs; mechanism: model the quality gained by giving the best starters more starts against public evidence of rest-day effects on velocity and results; baseline: a fixed five-man order, with skips only for injury; software: a schedule-aware start allocator, backtested on public game logs and Statcast velocity by days of rest.
public_rest_day_velocity_effect_estimate

Pinch-hitting and defensive substitution timing; owner: manager; decision: when to use a bench bat or defensive replacement in late innings, made daily; value at stake: win probability added in high-leverage situations; mechanism: compare the leverage-weighted value of using a bench player now against keeping him for a likely later spot; baseline: platoon-advantage substitutions plus routine late-inning defensive swaps; software: an in-game bench-usage model, backtested on public play-by-play by replaying substitution decisions.
Lineup batting-order optimization; this is likely a domain where software is unnecessary, because public research suggests the gap between a sensible order and an optimal one is small.

Spring training statistics; this is likely a domain where software is unnecessary, because samples are small and opponent quality varies, so the simple baseline of largely ignoring spring results is hard to beat.
